title: A brawl at Mary's Camp
summary: Clayton tells of a fight breaking out while the band played, hiding behind the music box while his brother-in-law sat on his head, and a young drummer fleeing.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: That's farther then. Guess there's no music down there now at Mary's? No, they cut up so bad I'm going to tell you. Last time I played down there, them boys got to fighting and we started playing music, thought it would stop them. Man, somebody put the lights out. Somebody throw the table, and the table come over there by me, and I sat down behind the music box and it paid off like a slot machine, you know when you hit the jackpot, ding-a-ling-a-ling. Because you grabbed the money. No, I sat there and my brother-in-law here in Baton Rouge, he'd come out and hear me play, and he'd sit on my head. I said sit right there, that's all right. He'd sit on my head. He'd sit on my head. I ain't never seen a man pack up a pair of drums and crawl out with him. See Abbey? Well Abbey was there. Abbey was there. That's right, he was playing with you when I was. I laughed until I cried. Abbey was running in the toilet there with his drums and he couldn't go no further, you know. He was just a boy now. But it was rough. Oh, it was rough down there. But we had the police when we come that next week and heist them all like a wrecker.
I remember a lot of young kids, like high school kids all the time I was there. That's right.
They sure they'd fight and kill. The women's too. Pick up tables, Troy, that one night.
And so I told my brother-in-law, I said you sit on my head, you ain't hurtin' me, I didn't want to get hit. I could stand his weights, you know.
